extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students or readers learning introductory symbolic/predicate logic
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory textbook material on propositional and predicate logic: definitions and evaluation rules for conditionals, biconditionals, connectives, quantifiers, negation, logical equivalence, truth tables, and basic inference rules, with examples and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of the conditional (P => Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: P => Q (read 'If P, then Q' or 'P implies Q') means that if P is true then Q must also be true; the only way the promise can be broken (i.e., be false) is if P is true but Q is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth table: false exactly in the case P true, Q false. Example: 'If you pass the final exam, then you will pass the course' — only false when you pass the exam but not the course. Consider P=>Q as a promise: it makes no claim about cases where P is false. In mathematics, a conditional with variables is understood with an implied universal quantifier (see 'implied universal quantifier').

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative English phrasings equivalent to 'If P, then Q'
rubrics_metrics.description: Many English constructions mean exactly the same as P => Q, e.g., 'If P, then Q.'; 'Q if P.'; 'Q whenever P.'; 'Q, provided that P.'; 'P is a sufficient condition for Q.'; 'Q is a necessary condition for P.'; 'P only if Q.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze each phrasing to verify it captures P => Q. Understand 'P is sufficient for Q' and 'Q is necessary for P' as restatements of the same implication. Be alert to subtle wording differences in everyday language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biconditional (P ↔ Q) meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: P ↔ Q (written P if and only if Q) means (P => Q) and (Q => P) both hold; equivalently P and Q are both true or both false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth table: true exactly when P and Q have the same truth value. Alternate phrasings: 'P is a necessary and sufficient condition for Q'; 'If P then Q, and conversely.' Use parentheses when combined with other connectives. Example: 'Integer a is even iff a is divisible by 2.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Two statements are logically equivalent if their truth values match up line-for-line in a truth table (they have the same truth table).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use equivalence to rewrite statements in potentially more useful forms. Example: P ↔ Q = (P ∧ Q) ∨ (¬P ∧ ¬Q). Another important equivalence: P => Q is equivalent to (¬Q) => (¬P) (the contrapositive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrapositive equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: P => Q is logically equivalent to (¬Q) => (¬P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equivalence is especially important because many theorems of form P => Q are easier to prove by proving the contrapositive. Verified by truth tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: DeMorgan's Laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Two standard equivalences for negation of conjunctions and disjunctions: ¬(P ∧ Q) = (¬P) ∨ (¬Q) and ¬(P ∨ Q) = (¬P) ∧ (¬Q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify via truth tables. Intuition: 'It is not the case that both P and Q' means 'at least one is false.' DeMorgan's laws are useful for transforming and negating statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation of a conditional
rubrics_metrics.description: The negation of a conditional ¬(P => Q) is logically equivalent to P ∧ ¬Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: 'P => Q is false' means there is an instance where P is true and Q is false. Use this when negating statements in proofs or exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifier semantics (∀ and ∃)
rubrics_metrics.description: The universal quantifier ∀ (read 'for all' or 'for every') and the existential quantifier ∃ (read 'there exists' or 'there is a') specify the quantity of the variable range: ∀x∈S, P(x) is true iff P(x) is true for every x∈S; ∃x∈S, P(x) is true iff P(x) is true for at least one x∈S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate English sentences carefully into quantified form. Examples: 'For every n∈Z, 2n is even' as ∀n∈Z, E(2n); 'There exists a subset X of N for which |X| = 5' as ∃X⊆N, |X| = 5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of quantifiers matters
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statement contains multiple quantifiers, reversing their order can change the meaning (e.g., ∀x ∃y vs ∃y ∀x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ∀x∈R ∃y∈R, y^3 = x is true, while ∃y∈R ∀x∈R, y^3 = x is false. Be careful translating and interpreting statements with more than one quantifier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation of quantified statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Negation swaps quantifiers and negates the predicate: ¬(∀x∈S, P(x)) = ∃x∈S, ¬P(x); ¬(∃x∈S, P(x)) = ∀x∈S, ¬P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these rules iteratively for multiple quantifiers. Example: Negating 'For every real x there exists y with y^3 = x' yields 'There exists x such that for all y, y^3 ≠ x.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied universal quantifier for conditionals with variables
rubrics_metrics.description: In mathematics, an unquantified conditional involving variables, P(x) => Q(x), is understood as the universally quantified statement ∀x∈S, P(x) => Q(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This convention is used because such conditionals are very common; e.g., 'If x is a multiple of 6 then x is even' is shorthand for ∀x∈Z, if x is a multiple of 6 then x is even.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translating English to symbolic logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate sentences into symbolic form to reveal logical structure; do not mechanically replace words (e.g., 'and'/'or') without checking intended meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'At least one of x and y is even' translates to (x is even) ∨ (y is even), not (x is even) ∧ (y is even). Use symbolic parsing to aid proofs and avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing truth tables for compound statements
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine truth values of complex expressions, list all combinations of atomic truth values and compute intermediate columns (helper columns) as needed, then combine them per connective rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helper columns are optional if confident. Examples include (P ∨ Q) ∧ ¬(P ∧ Q) (exclusive-or construction) and P ↔ (Q ∨ R) for three-variable tables with eight rows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses and operator precedence
rubrics_metrics.description: The negation operator ¬ binds tightly (e.g., ¬P ∨ Q means (¬P) ∨ Q, not ¬(P ∨ Q)); parentheses are necessary to disambiguate grouping in complex formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parentheses to make scope of negation and other connectives explicit, especially when combining quantifiers and multiple connectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common inference patterns (rules of inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain argument patterns let you derive conclusions from premises, e.g., modus ponens (from P => Q and P infer Q), conjunction introduction/elimination (from P and Q infer P ∧ Q; from P ∧ Q infer P), and disjunction introduction (from P infer P ∨ Q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These patterns are justified by truth tables and are the basic building blocks in proofs. The text presents several such inferences as tabular examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using logical equivalences to simplify proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite statements using known equivalences (DeMorgan's laws, contraposition, distributive-like identities) to obtain forms more amenable to proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: proving P => Q may be easier by proving the contrapositive (¬Q) => (¬P); equivalences can also expose hidden structure and allow algebraic manipulation of logical expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful natural-language practice tips
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid casual-language mistakes that change logical meaning (e.g., 'All students do not pay full tuition' vs 'Not all students pay full tuition').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In mathematical contexts, precision is required: prefer 'Not all' instead of 'All ... not' when you mean existence of exceptions. Practice translating idiomatic sentences provided in exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negating compound examples via DeMorgan and quantifier rules
rubrics_metrics.description: To negate sentences like 'You can solve it by factoring or with the quadratic formula' (P ∨ Q), apply DeMorgan to get ¬P ∧ ¬Q; for quantified compounds, apply quantifier-negation rules in sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work through examples: negation of 'The square of every real number is nonnegative' becomes 'There exists a real number whose square is negative.' Use the provided exemplar problems to internalize the procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercises and internalization recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth tables for a, v, ¬, =>, ↔ should be memorized and internalized; practice translating, negating, and making truth tables for increasingly complex statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes internalization by repeated exercises; helper columns may be omitted once comfortable. Logic should remain a background tool used mentally when reading/writing proofs.
